title: A soap bubble has no colour of its own: the rainbow is its thickness
body: A soap film is a sheet of water about a micrometre thick, comparable to the wavelength of visible light. Light reflecting off its front surface meets light reflecting off its back surface, and depending on the thickness the two waves either reinforce or cancel for each colour. So the swirls on a bubble are a **map of its thickness**, shifting as the film drains. Where it thins below about 100 nanometres the reflections cancel almost completely and the film looks black, yet it can stay intact for minutes.

slides.alt: A light ray hits a thin soap film. One reflection comes from the front surface and a second from the back surface; the two reflected rays travel side by side and overlap. The film thickness is marked.
slides.caption: Two reflections, one from each surface, overlap. Thickness decides which colours survive.

slides.label: thickness of a ‘Newton black film’, the thinnest kind of soap film
slides.text: Common black films are around 50 nm. In both, the two surfaces have practically snapped together, pinching out the water between them.

slides.heading: Why a bubble is round
slides.text: A soap film pulls itself as small as it can. For a given volume of air, the shape with the least surface is a sphere, a fact proved in 1884 by H. A. Schwarz. Blow a bubble through a square frame and it still comes out round.

slides.question: Why can a patch of soap film look black?
options: It is too thin to reflect light in step
slides.explanation: Below about 100 nm the front and back reflections cancel almost completely for every colour, so the patch sends almost no light back to your eye.
